meta.ogDescription: Attributed to Cesar Chavez and published by the UFW, but pinned to no primary source — and definitively not from the 1984 speech everyone cites.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1927–1993 · American labor leader, co-founder of the United Farm Workers
answer.sourceLine: The United Farm Workers — the union Chavez co-founded — publishes this as his words, and President Obama quoted it in an official 2012 proclamation. But no speech, letter, or interview containing it has ever been produced, and the address it is usually credited to, the Commonwealth Club speech of 9 November 1984, demonstrably does not contain it.

source.heading: Where the quote actually lives

docMeta.dd: Education of the Heart: Cesar Chavez in his own words

Not identified — no date, venue, or transcript located

source.excerpt:
Community

“We cannot seek achievement for ourselves and forget about progress and prosperity for our community…Our ambitions must be broad enough to include the aspirations and needs of others, for their sakes and for our own.”

“When we are really honest with ourselves we must admit that our lives are all that really belong to us. So, it how we use our lives that determines what kind of men we are.”
trail: The quote's institutional home is the United Farm Workers' own compilation, Education of the Heart: Cesar Chavez in his own words ↗. It prints the line under the heading “Community” — with no date, venue, or transcript, exactly like every other quote on the page.
Its highest-profile appearance is President Obama's Cesar Chavez Day proclamation of March 23, 2012 ↗, which quotes it verbatim but introduces it only with “He told us” and cites no source.

The speech usually named as the origin is ruled out. The Address to the Commonwealth Club of 9 November 1984 ↗ does not contain the line — its complete 3,491-word text never uses the words “achievement,” “ambition,” “prosperity,” or “aspiration” — and an independent transcript ↗ confirms it.

No specialist has ever traced it. Wikiquote's Chavez page ↗, which documents four major speeches from 1965 to 1990, does not carry the line in any section, sourced or otherwise; Quote Investigator has no entry on it.
source.excerptNote: This is how the quote appears on the UFW's own page — grouped under the heading “Community,” sandwiched between unrelated remarks, with no date or source attached to any of them. Note the ellipsis in the middle: it is the UFW's own, and it marks a splice between two separate statements. There is no fuller original context to show, because no original has been found.

source.rightsNote: Chavez lived 1927–1993, so any words of his fall well after the 1931 public-domain cutoff, and the UFW page carrying this quote states plainly ↗ that “The Cesar E. Chavez Foundation is the intellectual property owner of Cesar’s name, voice, image, and likeness, speeches and writings,” directing anyone reproducing them to seek permission. The specific source work has never been identified, so its exact publication date is unknown — but nothing about this line puts it in the public domain.

author.name: Cesar Chavez
author.heading: Who was Cesar Chavez?
author.metaLine: 1927–1993 · American labor leader & co-founder of the United Farm Workers
author.bio: Cesar Chavez was an American farm worker, labor organizer, and civil rights leader who co-founded the National Farm Workers Association — later the United Farm Workers — with Dolores Huerta in 1962. Through grape boycotts, marches, and long public fasts, he built the first enduring farm workers' union in the United States and made “Si Se Puede” a rallying cry far beyond the fields. His rhetoric consistently subordinated individual success to collective advancement, which is precisely why this quote sits so plausibly in his mouth — and why so few people have thought to check it.

misattribution.heading: What's actually wrong here
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Chavez himself is not the problem — his own union publishes the line as his. What's wrong is the citation that travels with it, and the impression that this is a sentence he spoke in one breath.

items.who: “Address to the Commonwealth Club,” San Francisco, 9 November 1984
items.why: This is the source most often attached to the quote, and it is demonstrably wrong. The complete text of the November 9, 1984 address ↗ runs 3,491 words and never once uses the words “achievement,” “ambition,” “prosperity,” or “aspiration.” An independent transcript ↗ agrees, and UFW's own page about that speech ↗ does not quote the line either.

Nearly every version in circulation — including the UFW's own ↗ — carries an ellipsis between the two halves. That mark is doing real work: it joins two separate remarks. The seamless one-sentence version quoted from podiums is a compression, not a transcript.

The aggregators pass it along with nothing behind it. A-Z Quotes ↗ lists it with no citation; PassItOn ↗ credits only “Cesar Chavez, Civil rights activist”; and Goodreads ↗ — which warns that its quotes are community-added and unverified — names no work.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is very likely Chavez in substance: the United Farm Workers ↗, the union he co-founded, publishes it as his words, and it echoes what he argued for thirty years. But no speech, letter, or interview containing it has ever been produced — and the 1984 address everyone cites plainly does not.

context.heading: Why this one is hard to pin down
lead: Chavez is not a typical fake-quote magnet. He was a working organizer, not an essayist, and much of what he said was said out loud — at rallies, on picket lines, in union halls, in hundreds of interviews across thirty years. A great deal of it was never transcribed, and what was transcribed is scattered across union archives rather than a collected edition. That leaves a genuine gap between “he probably said this” and “here is where he said it.”

This quote lives in that gap. It carries the endorsement of the institutions closest to him — his own union publishes it, and a sitting president put it in a proclamation — while resting on no citable document at all. The result is a line that is almost certainly authentic in substance and completely unverifiable in fact.
context.detailsSummary: How the ellipsis gives it away
detailsBody: Look closely at how the quote is printed, including on the UFW's own page: “…prosperity for our community…Our ambitions must be broad enough…” That ellipsis sits between the two halves in virtually every version in circulation, and it is not decorative — it marks a splice. Whoever assembled the compilation was joining material that did not originally run together.

This matters for anyone quoting it. The smooth, single-sentence version that appears on posters and in commencement speeches is a compression of two separate remarks, not a sentence Chavez ever delivered in one breath. Reproducing it without the ellipsis quietly upgrades an edited compilation into a transcript.

It also explains why the Commonwealth Club citation could spread so easily. Once a quote has no source of its own, it tends to get adopted by the most famous speech in the author's catalogue — and Chavez's 1984 Commonwealth Club address is the speech everyone knows.
context.pull: Endorsed by his own union, quoted by a president, and traceable to nothing.
